description: I am a programmer who is passionate about hackathons.
summary: I developed MoonCrux, a mission-planning web tool that compares landing sites at the Moon's south pole, where the Sun and the Earth sit right on the horizon and a single ridge can leave a lander without power or contact. It directly addresses the challenge by showing, for any landing date in 2027, whether each site will have sunlight and a direct link to Earth, combining Sun and Earth positions from NASA's JPL Horizons system with the real terrain horizon computed from LRO LOLA elevation data. Beyond that, it places science next to engineering: each site is scored for power, communication and proximity to permanently shadowed regions, where water ice is expected, and a delay control shows instantly how the best site changes when the launch slips. Its sunlight results stay within about four percentage points of NASA's own illumination maps. It does not just show where the Sun and the Earth are; it shows which site still works when the plan changes.
details:
MoonCrux: Your launch just slipped three weeks. Which landing site still works?

At the Moon's south pole, the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon and the Earth rises and sets behind the hills. **A single ridge decides whether a lander has power and whether it can talk to Earth.** The data to answer that exists, but it is spread across specialist tools, one scenario at a time. When a schedule changes, comparing alternatives is slow.

What is MoonCrux?

Named after Crux, the Southern Cross, the constellation long used to find south. MoonCrux is a mission-planning web tool, used on Earth before launch. You choose a landing day, a mission duration and a launch delay, and it tells you which south-pole sites work, why, and what changes if the date moves.

How it works

Sun and Earth. Hourly positions for every hour of 2027, as seen from each site, from NASA's JPL Horizons system.

Real horizon. A 360-degree terrain profile for each site, computed from LRO LOLA elevation data with lunar curvature, at 20 m resolution near the site and out to 200 km.

Visibility. The Sun or the Earth is visible when any part of its disc clears the terrain in its direction, the same convention as NASA's illumination maps.

Decision rules. Sun visible at landing, longest period of darkness, share of sunlight, terrain slope and direct contact with Earth. The rules are fixed, shown on screen and adjustable by the user.

What you see

A 3D view of the south pole, lit by the real direction of the Sun at the landing instant, so shadows move when the date moves. Site cards with an engineering score, a science score, a verdict and the rule that decided it. A delay control: slip the launch and watch the ranking change. For each site, the horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth paths and a mission timeline of sunlight and contact.

The difference: science next to engineering, on a real date

Science teams want to land close to permanently shadowed regions, where water ice is expected. Engineering teams want sunlight and a link to Earth. MoonCrux shows both in one view and points to the best overall site. And it evaluates dates, not averages: **a site with 87% average sunlight can still be dark on your landing day.**

What the data shows

With the default rules and a 14-day mission, on 71 of the 352 possible landing days in 2027 no site is viable, and on 110 dates a 21-day slip moves the best site to a different one. In our default scenario, landing on January 10 favors Shackleton rim; three weeks later it is no longer viable and Connecting ridge takes its place. Two points 2.8 km apart at Shackleton receive 87% and 11% average sunlight.

Checked against NASA

Our share of sunlit hours in 2027 differs from NASA's 18.6-year average illumination maps by -0.5 to +4.1 percentage points at the five sites, with no tuning. The comparison and its limits are shown in the tool.

What i considered

Correctness: the same lunar reference frame and sphere for positions and terrain, and automated tests for every calculation. Fairness: every site point is chosen by the same rule, the most-illuminated pixel of its NASA region. Honesty about limits: one year of data, five fixed points that represent the best case of each region, direct line of sight only; trajectory, thermal environment and surface hazards are not covered. Accessibility: color-blind-safe palette, verdicts never shown by color alone, keyboard navigation, English and Portuguese.

Tools

Python for the data pipeline; TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js for the interface. A static site with no server, hosted on Vercel.

What comes next

Any coordinate and whole-region evaluation, several years of data, relay-satellite coverage, and the same method applied to Mars.

Source code: https://github.com/Aquno/NasaSpaceApps

Independent hackathon project, not a NASA product.
